main.summary: The Rebirth Mantra (Wangsheng Zhou) is a dharani that takes refuge in Amitabha Buddha and prays for rebirth in the Western Pure Land. It is one of the 'Ten Short Mantras' of Chinese Buddhism and is traditionally recited in the morning and evening services of Pure Land practitioners.
main.translation: This mantra is the Sanskrit sounds written in Chinese characters. By tradition it is recited, not translated word by word, and the practice rests on sound and a steady mind. Its general sense may be understood like this. It begins by taking refuge in and paying homage to the Tathagata Amitabha (「南無阿彌多婆夜，哆他伽多夜」: homage to the Limitless Light, to the Tathagata). It then praises Amitabha's nectar-like teaching and boundless merit with the repeated word 「阿彌唎哆」 (amrita: nectar, the deathless). It closes with 「娑婆訶」 (svaha), marking fulfilment. Teachers explain the lines in between in different ways, so no forced translation of them is given here.

glossary.note: 'Zhou' stands for the Sanskrit dharani or mantra, meaning 'total retention', the power to hold countless meanings together. Chinese Buddhism keeps the original sounds in transcription and does not translate them.
A transcription of the Sanskrit namo: to take refuge in, pay homage to, entrust oneself to. It is placed before the names of buddhas and bodhisattvas.
The Sanskrit amitabhaya, 'to the One of Limitless Light', that is, Amitabha Buddha. Amitabha (limitless light) and Amitayus (limitless life) are two names for the same Buddha.
The Sanskrit tathagataya, 'to the Tathagata'. Tathagata, 'one who has thus come', is one of the ten titles of a Buddha.
The Sanskrit amrita, 'nectar' or sweet dew, and by extension the deathless: lasting awakening and liberation. It is the word that returns again and again in the mantra.
The Sanskrit svaha, often found at the close of a mantra, meaning fulfilment, good fortune and completion: may what is wished come true.

main.background: The mantra comes from the dharani on 'Uprooting All Karmic Obstacles and Gaining Rebirth in the Pure Land', translated by Gunabhadra in the Liu Song dynasty (420-479) of the Southern Dynasties. It was later attached to the Amitabha Sutra and gathered into the 'Ten Short Mantras', and it spread widely in Pure Land devotion after the Tang and Song dynasties. A few characters of the transcription differ between printed editions; this copybook follows the usual recitation text.
